### Proposal

According to estimates by AI labs, benchmarking and evaluating takes around 10% to 15% of total model training time (Olmo-3, Llama). Fast, granular, and trustworthy benchmarking is crucial for EDU-LLM due to the sheer number of novel hypotheses being tested. We propose a skill-based Computerized Adaptive Test, attempting to show a 100x reduction in the number of items required in a diagnostic to report a predicted accuracy on a specific skill in benchmarks, while holding a similar level of precision as full-length benchmarks.  

### Current Methodologies

ATLAS: [https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04689v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04689v2)  
tinyBenchmarks: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.14992](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.14992)  
FLUID: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11106](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11106)  
Critical Review on Current Evaluation Methods: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04069](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04069) 

General Benchmarking:  
The current standard for benchmarking is just doing large runs on commonly known benchmarks. The following is a compiled list of issues with existing benchmarks:

- Reproducibility is hard, prompting strategies, decoding settings, and LLM as judge evaluators can make it hard to reproduce benchmark results.   
- There are data integrity issues due to outdated or otherwise incorrect information along with contamination in training sets.   
- Diversity, coverage, and generalizability are not tested properly by benchmarks, as shown by discrepancies in results.  
- Human evaluation doesn’t always agree with the automated benchmarks 

A few of these issues will still persist with our method, our biggest strength can be transparency. We are aiming to be honest about our prompting, decoding, and other evaluation strategies so our results are reproducible. At the end of the day we are predicting performance on pre-existing benchmarks, while aiming to speed up evaluation and increase granularity of skill-analysis.

Tutoring Benchmarks:  
Pedagogy Benchmark: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.18710](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.18710)  
TutorBench:[https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.02663](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.02663)

Pedagogy Benchmark is based on a teachers exam dataset that was cleaned and validated, ran on many frontier models and open sourced models. 899 questions with a 95% confidence interval, all of the questions were reviewed by an expert. However this has limitations as it only uses one source which was translated and came from a Chilean exam, meaning it has bias in that direction. It’s also only MCQs which limits the ability to diagnose pedagogical behavior properly.  It is a useful source bank but it needs proper MIRT calibration, CAT compression, and free-response questions added in. 

CAT benchmarking:  
Computer Adaptive Testing for LLM benchmarking is still a relatively new idea, and definitely not widely adopted. TinyBenchmarks paper has gained popularity and shown the potential for dramatic reduction in number of items required for accurate benchmarking. However, our proposal is using the CAT system from ATLAS which preliminary research has shown to improve further both in the trustworthiness/granularity of results and amount of items required.  
The following is a high level overview of the current process for CAT for benchmarking:

**Data Construction & IRT Calibration**  
Data is collected from major benchmarks, aiming to get good coverage of skills. Get a list of open source models that will be used to calibrate the IRT model. Filter items in the benchmark, to make sure you only keep items that are able to distinguish model’s scores by a significant amount on the full benchmarks. Usually models are stratified by token size, however we have a defined parameter range so we will only get models from this range. Make a Train/Test split within the models chosen to evaluate the accuracy of the IRT model. Divide items into subsets, calibrate using models as “common persons”, the benchmark scores being used to align and merge the different subsets. This provides for a quick IRT calibration.

**Adaptive Diagnostic**  
The adaptive diagnostic process is very similar to existing CAT applications. Minimal change to existing methodology will be made, using model inference to actually make the model take the diagnostic. The methodology is described in detail in **Figure 1**.

### Proposed Changes

Instead of only pulling from general frontier LLM benchmarks, we will also calibrate on questions from benchmarks targeted towards tutoring and other educational capabilities. While current research has shown that reasoning benchmarks such as MMLU can be reduced while maintaining accuracy, we want to see if this holds for benchmarks more targeted towards education.

The 3PL IRT model used by ATLAS, the framework we are primarily working off of, is generally a dichotomous model. This means that each answer choice is either right or wrong.

Furthermore, current methods for adaptive testing in benchmarking approximate one overall ability score. We propose assigning items within the testing set to more specific skills, for instance generating explanations vs hints, and measuring ability for each skill. With this, our benchmark will be able to evaluate multiple more distinct capabilities as opposed to overall capability.

### Implementation Details

Our Multidimensional IRT Model will estimate an ability vector, Theta, with 4 skills:

- Content knowledge  
  - Correct and factual information on a subject   
- Diagnosis  
  - Identify specific misconceptions or missing knowledge on learner side  
- Scaffolding  
  - Inform without giving away answer, giving hints that advance learner progress  
- Adaptability  
  - Change explanations and strategies given prior work, stated confusions, unsuccessful prior explanations to ensure personalized learning

These dimensions are hypotheses rather than assumed to be independent

**Q-Matrix:** A Q-Matrix is a mapping of items/questions to the skills required to answer it correctly. Used for multidimensional IRT. Here is a starting example q matrix, we’ll synthetically generate rows for each question(refer below for methodology). 

| Scenario | Content | Diagnosis | Scaffolding | Adaptation |
| :---- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Explain a subject concept accurately | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Identify misconception demonstrated in a student’s work | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Select a next-step hint after the misconception is provided. | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Rewrite an explanation for a learner who found the original one too technical | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Identify a misconception and select an appropriate next step  | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Revise a hint after the learner reports that the first hint did not help  | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

Skills will only be marked with a 1 if it is absolutely necessary for the scenario to be executed properly. As you can see, question items can be multidimensional or one dimensional. We will split question items as 60% multidimensional scenarios and 40% one dimensional skill questions. 

**Synthetic Q-Matrix Generation:**  
Initial Q-Matrix is generated with an LLM given sample row from TutorBench dataset. item and answer choices, correct answer with rationale, the definition of the four skills, and positive/negative labeling examples.   
For each 1 it proposes to place in the matrix, it must give evidence from the item and an explanation for why the correct answer cannot be reached without that skill. It also needs a counterfactual describing why a model without the skill couldn’t determine the correct answer.

Once the 1’s are filled in, they’ll be reassessed by two independent LLM verifiers and, on a small subset of samples, two human reviewers, with positive labels only kept on unanimous results. There will also be a sample of 0 labels to check the false negative rate. All of the prompts and details will be kept for reproducibility. 

After finalizing a Q-Matrix, we will compare the provisional multidimensional model against unidimensional IRT and see if the skills are actually distinguishable. Then we will evaluate alternative q-matrix mappings to compare results. 

**CAT model:**

Initially our CAT model will use Random selection with uniform sampling to choose questions as Latent Ability isn’t determined. From there, it will compute fisher information and choose from the highest 5 information items for what appears next.

Note that since we are extending this framework to be multidimensional, fisher information can be represented by a dxd matrix. The next item chosen will be one that maximizes the determinant of the updated information matrix. This criterion is called D-optimality.

We will follow the general pipeline used by ATLAS, but adapt the mathematical models we use to fit with a Multidimensional Graded Response Model (M-GRM). This adaptation is mainly in the item choosing section, as we’ll choose items based on which skill has the highest error.   
Refer to this diagram:  
**![][image1]**  
**Figure 1: Adaptive Testing Model (ATLAS)**

**Stopping Rule:**

When each skill has at least 15 observations and a standard error \<= 0.3. Additionally, there must be at least 40 overall observations across everything with a general Standard Error of \<= 0.2. 

### Experiments

**Base Reproducibility Test**  
Take 1 benchmark, recreate ATLAS methodology, and use a held out test set of models to verify the prediction accuracy of the CAT diagnostic.

**Multidimensional Prerequisite Test**  
Use LLM’s to generate the Q-matrices for all test items across all benchmarks. Run a test to see the effect of “temperature”, “difference in prompt”, and type of LLM on the matrices created. Then compare with human created matrices, to deliver the exact confidence interval of error introduced.

**Multidimensional Reproducibility Test**  
Calibrate Multidimensional IRT model, and use held out test set of models AND skill specific benchmark items, give a clear statistical prediction accuracy per skill with confidence interval.

### Success Metrics

Correlation of .7 \- .85 with TutorBench and correlation of .4 to .7 to general frontier LLM benchmarks. Median length of this benchmark should be \<= 75 items, with a 90th percentile length being \<= 100 items.

**Theoretical Ideal Length vs Correlation table:**

| Item amount | Ideal Correlation with Full Benchmark Bank |
| :---: | :---: |
| 10 | \>=0.7 |
| 25 | \>=0.85 |
| 50 | \>=0.92 |
| 75 | \>=0.95 |
| 100 | \>=0.97 |
